query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: An integrated metadynamics simulation approach enhanced by machine-learning‐optimized interatomic potentials under isothermal–isobaric conditions can accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a broad range of high‐entropy alloy compositions.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase high-entropy alloy solid solutions with disordered multi-element configurations (e.g., equiatomic fcc or bcc systems).
generation.intervention: Application of enhanced free energy landscape sampling via integrated metadynamics simulations combined with machine-learning‐optimized interatomic potentials.
generation.conditions: Simulations performed in an isothermal–isobaric ensemble over a representative range of high-entropy alloy compositions, covering various crystal structures.
generation.structural_mediator: Detailed mapping of the complete Gibbs free energy surfaces that capture subtle structural transitions during melting.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced sampling reduces kinetic barriers, enabling accurate resolution of the free energy differences associated with melting and fusion events, thereby capturing the enthalpic and entropic contributions accurately.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method is expected to yield predictions of melting temperature, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, and volume changes at melting within approximately 5-10% of experimental values, while reliably capturing key liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
generation.baseline: Traditional simplified models and limited-range simulations that provide less accurate estimates and lack comprehensive free energy surface mapping.
generation.boundary: The approach is most applicable to high-entropy alloys where high-quality machine-learning potentials are available; extreme compositions or systems with poorly trained potentials may result in larger deviations.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the error margins at the extremities of composition space and at very high pressures, where potential inaccuracies in the machine learning potentials and sampling challenges may lead to deviations beyond the expected 5-10%.

falsification_experiment.design: Select several high-entropy alloy samples with well-characterized experimental melting properties. Perform integrated metadynamics simulations under isothermal–isobaric conditions for these alloys using the proposed machine-learning‐optimized potentials. Compare the computed melting temperature, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting to the benchmark experimental values.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simulation predictions deviate by more than 10% from the experimentally measured values across multiple compositions, then the proposed approach is deemed falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Recently, a new alloy design concept based on entropic contributions to the thermodynamic landscape, rather than cohesive energy, was proposed, which was subsequently extended to non-metallic systems such as multicomponent oxides. This strategy was explored by deliberately incorporating five or more elemental species into a single lattice with random site occupancy. Due to the engineered configuration disorder, these entropy-stabilized solid solution alloys, that is, high-entropy alloys (HEAs), usually show a single-phase structure with high symmetry and extremely attractive properties. Among various reported HEAs in literature, the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy (also termed as Cantor's alloy) is a prototype fcc (face-centred-cubic) HEA, which possesses ultrahigh fracture toughness and large ductility, even at cryogenic temperatures. It is generally believed that HEA lattices are severely distorted and atomic diffusion is extremely sluggish due to the chemical complexity and packing disorder. In this work the heat capacity, entropy, enthalpy and Gibbs free energy of six different single-phase solid solution alloys (three fcc-alloys, two bcc-alloys and one hcp-alloy) were experimentally determined and investigated over a wide temperature range. At room temperature (RT), molar heat capacities of the studied alloys are close to 3R, in accordance with the Dulong-Petit law. The measured RT heat capacities of the studied alloys are in good agreement with the heat capacities calculated using the rule of mixture of pure elements. Thermal entropy and thermal enthalpy increase while the thermal part of the Gibbs free energy decreases with an increase in temperature. The temperature dependence of these quantities is the strongest for the hcp alloy and weakest for the bcc alloys, with the fcc alloys showing intermediate behavior. For the alloys with the same crystal structure, the thermal contributions to the Gibbs free energy do not depend on the number and concentration of the alloying elements. The third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure Cr and V in both the liquid and A2 phases were established. By applying these expressions, the thermodynamic properties down to 0 K and thermal vacancy near the melting point can be well described. Besides, the lattice stability of Cr and V over the whole temperature range can be guaranteed. Based on the third-generation Gibbs energy expressions of pure elements, the Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems were thermodynamically assessed by considering the reviewed phase equilibria and thermodynamic data with the CALPHAD approach. A strategy to estimate the Gibbs energy of Laves phase was proposed by combining the theoretically computed and experimentally measured thermodynamic properties as well as semiempirical relation. Such a method was applied to C14 and C15 Laves phases in Ta-Cr and Ta-V binary systems. The calculated phase diagrams and thermodynamic properties showed nice agreement with the measured ones. Significant improvements can be observed at low temperatures compared with those from the second-generation thermodynamic descriptions, indicating the high reliability of the present thermodynamic descriptions.
